item.title: Putin Reignited a Dispute With Japan. This Town Is Stuck in the Middle.
item.description:
The news traveled quickly on a paradisiacal summer day in Nemuro, a remote fishing town in northern Japan. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, in a show of strength, had made a surprise visit to a nearby chain of islands that both Russia and Japan claim.

At Nemuro’s City Hall, Mayor Masatoshi Ishigaki was concerned. For decades, the town’s residents have promoted Japan’s claims to the snow-capped island chain that Mr. Putin was visiting, with patriotic museums, billboards (“Give it back!”) and monuments.

But Nemuro, on the northern island of Hokkaido, also depends on Russia for trade and fishing rights, and Mr. Ishigaki worried any flare-up could hurt the economy.

“When friction arises between Japan and Russia, the pain is felt here immediately,” he said inside his office at City Hall, where the disputed islands loom in the distance on clear days.

The fight over the archipelago, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and in Russia as the southern Kuril Islands, has festered since 1945, when Moscow seized the territory from Japan in the final weeks of World War II. Japan has pushed Russia for years to relinquish control of at least two of four inhabited islands. But Moscow has resisted, and the two sides have yet to sign a peace treaty formally ending the war.

Now Mr. Putin has revived the issue — an effort, analysts say, to put pressure on Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s hawkish prime minister, and to rally nationalist sentiment in Russia.Mr. Putin has increased the frequency and scale of military exercises in the seas near Nemuro. He has said that Russia’s claims to the islands are a “reality” that has been “enshrined in international documents.” He has attacked Japan for maintaining economic sanctions on Russia that were imposed after his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. And he has encouraged criticism of Tokyo; Russia recently unveiled a statue showing a Soviet soldier smashing the chrysanthemum seal of Japan’s imperial family.

On his visit last month to the disputed islands, the first in his quarter-century rule, Mr. Putin ate caviar and toured a seafood-processing plant. He was shown on Russian state television meeting with adoring crowds under a bright sun; one woman told him “the weather is smiling on you.”

Ms. Takaichi has called Mr. Putin’s visit “absolutely unacceptable” and said he “hurt the feelings of the Japanese people.” Her government has protested a new world map that shows Russia and the disputed islands in the same shade of yellow.

Nowhere are the tensions more deeply felt than in Nemuro, a serene town of about 22,000 that is known for icy winters, kaleidoscopic sunrises and the bright-red spiny king crabs harvested on its shores.

Nemuro lies just a few miles from the southernmost part of the disputed islands, which are part of an archipelago stretching from the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula in eastern Russia to Hokkaido at the top of Japan.

Like many rural Japanese towns, Nemuro has suffered from long-term demographic decline; its population is now about half of its peak of about 50,000 in the 1960s. Many young people have left for jobs and schools in Tokyo and other cities, as the economy has been hit by Russian-imposed limits on fishing for salmon and trout, and as trade has dwindled.

Russian sailors used to abound in Nemuro — so much so that the local schools still teach Russian, and stores cater to Russian visitors, who once came in search of refrigerators, ovens, bicycles, smartphones and televisions. Nemuro’s ports still display posters in fading Cyrillic type, including one that says: “Dear foreign sailors! Please practice safe navigation!”

But as relations between Japan and Russia have deteriorated in recent years, many Russians have stayed at home, hurting business at Nemuro’s restaurants, bars and seafood processors. For those who still come — hawking sea urchin, mackerel and kelp — it can be lonely.

“It feels like we’re the last of the Russians,” said Alexey Dudka, a sailor from the nearby Russian port town of Kholmsk, who was stopping in Nemuro for repairs on his ship. “It’s a ghost town now.”

Despite its links to Russia, Nemuro has long been on the front lines of Japan’s efforts to win back the disputed islands, roughly the size of the state of Delaware. The town is filled with nationalistic posters that proclaim, “The Northern Territories are a Japanese territory.” A museum shows ancient books and maps meant to prove Japan’s longstanding ties to the islands. Japan traces its claims to the islands to the 17th century.

The patriotic mission in Nemuro has traditionally been led by former residents of the islands from Japan, but their ranks are dwindling. There are now about 4,700 living former residents in Japan, down from about 17,000 who were expelled by the Soviet Union at the end of World War II. They have an average age of about 90.

Hiroshi Tokunou, 92, was 11 in 1945 when Soviet troops occupied the islands. After living and studying alongside the Soviets for a brief period, he and his relatives were sent to an internment camp, to make way for incoming Soviet families. In 1947, they were allowed to return to Hokkaido.

Mr. Tokunou said Mr. Putin “operates with a kind of cunning shrewdness,” adding that Japan should be firm in dealing with Russia. But, he said, “We also have to leave room for better relations in the future, for a rekindling down the line.” He said he was concerned the issue might fade if it is not taken up by Nemuro’s younger residents, who he worries have a “different way of thinking.”

Outside a local supermarket, Natsumi Nishita, 34, said it was “hard to get the same level of passion” as Nemuro’s elders about the dispute. Ms. Nishita, an English teacher at a cram school in Nemuro, said there were more important issues to worry about, like the economy.

“What Putin did was just a little thing that happened — a political appeal,” she said. “People here don’t think it’s a big deal.”

Mr. Ishigaki, the mayor of Nemuro, said he feels the islands are a missed opportunity for Japan; the local government estimates it could generate roughly $462 million each year in revenues from fisheries, seafood processing and other activities if it controlled the islands.

“We want to resolve this issue while we are still alive,” Mr. Ishigaki, 75, said.

Ms. Takaichi has refrained from penalizing Moscow over Mr. Putin’s visit, as Japan manages acute energy concerns because of the war in Iran. Japan imports about 10 percent of its liquefied natural gas from Russia.

Ms. Takaichi’s government had seemed interested in improving relations with Mr. Putin, restarting trade and cultural visits to Moscow earlier this year, despite some objections from European allies. But Mr. Putin’s visit has cast doubt on those efforts.

“Russia tends not to reciprocate when another side makes unilateral concessions,” said James D.J. Brown, a professor of political science at Temple University in Tokyo. “Instead, they double down on pressure.”

Every year, Nemuro holds ceremonies to remember ancestors buried on the islands. These rituals used to take place, with Moscow’s blessing, at cemeteries in the disputed territories.

But after Japan imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022, Mr. Putin suspended those visits and they are now performed at sea.

On a stormy morning this month, Taiko Kodama, 81, a retiree and activist who was born in the disputed territories, boarded a ferry to take part in a ceremony.

Aboard the boat, called the Puffin, she said a prayer for her parents and grandparents, and laid flowers in their memory. She keeps two black stones from the islands inside her purse to remember her homeland, which she fled in 1947, when she was 3. She said she still remembers the smell of kelp there.

“Our homes were taken from us unfairly,” she said. “We have to speak from our hearts.”

item.title: Why a Law to Help Prisoners Became a New Sectarian Flashpoint in Lebanon
item.description:
When President Joseph Aoun of Lebanon signed an amnesty law this month to free some inmates and reduce sentences for others, it was meant to ease prison overcrowding and relieve an overwhelmed judicial system.

Instead, the law has exposed and deepened political divisions in Lebanon, which has long been mired in political and economic crises and sectarianism.

In a country divided among Christian, Muslim and Druse communities, the legislation became a balancing act between competing interests, with various groups questioning accommodations made for others. Few are satisfied by the result.

Lebanon’s Constitutional Council, the highest authority in disputes about laws, suspended the law this month after some lawmakers filed an appeal challenging it. Prisoners protested the suspension, with some launching a hunger strike. The Council is expected to issue a final decision by early October.

Here’s what to know about the law and what some hoped to gain from it.

The new law was intended to deal with packed prisons and an overstretched judiciary, with many held for years without trial. It is unclear how many of them would be eligible for release under the new law.

Many prisoners have serious health problems and receive inadequate medical care, and some have died awaiting trial, according to Mahmoud Abdalla, a member of the Committee of the Families of Prisoners in Lebanon, a nonprofit advocating for the humane treatment of inmates.

Mohamed Beiruti, from the northern city of Tripoli, said his son has been incarcerated for years on suspicions of belonging to a terrorist group, without being charged and with limited access to a lawyer. “They took away every right from him,” said Mr. Beiruti, who said the accusations against his son were unfounded.

The law combines a broad amnesty for some prisoners with sentence reductions for others.

It replaces the death penalty with 28 years in prison, and life imprisonment with hard labor and a sentence of 17 years. It also reduces other sentences by a third, with special provisions for intentional or premeditated murder committed under certain aggravating circumstances.

The law excludes offenses including human trafficking, terrorist financing and repeat drug offenses.

It also excludes amnesty for Lebanese who collaborated with and fled to Israel — considered treason in Lebanon — after the Israeli military withdrew from the south of the country in 2000, following almost 20 years of occupation. However, the amnesty covers Lebanese who also fled to Israel but who did not serve in a military or security capacity.

The law was championed by Sunni Muslim lawmakers seeking to free Islamist detainees, many of them Sunni, who fought the Lebanese military over a decade ago. The lawmakers argued that the detainees had been unfairly convicted by military courts that were biased against Sunnis, at a time when Hezbollah, the Shiite Muslim militia, and its allies wielded greater influence in Lebanon.

“We needed a new page,” said Mohammad Sablouh, a human rights lawyer who has represented dozens of Sunni Islamist prisoners. Lebanon was for years, he said, “a country of gangs, not laws,” hence the need for “a national general amnesty law.”

Lebanon’s military opposed the law over concerns that it could free or reduce the sentences of people convicted of killing soldiers, according to Lebanon’s defense minister, Michel Menassa.

For the Shiite community, the priority was amnesty for Shiites detained in drug-related cases, especially smallholder cannabis farmers in the northeastern Baalbek-Hermel region. Supporters of the law said widespread poverty in the area had left residents with few options but to grow the crop.

Hussein Hajj Hassan, a lawmaker representing Hezbollah, said the effort to relieve pressure on prisons had turned into a political fight. “Unfortunately, like everything in Lebanon, it is politicized, sectarianized and ideologized,” he said.

For Lebanon’s Christian community, the aim was to provide legal relief to Lebanese who fled to Israel after its military withdrew from southern Lebanon in 2000. Some were members or supporters of the South Lebanon Army, a militia that worked with Israel during the occupation.

Tony Abu Jamra, a Christian, left Lebanon for Mexico through Israel after the Israeli occupation, saying he and many others fled for fear of being branded traitors despite having no ties to Israel. He returned to his hometown, Marjayoun, in southern Lebanon, in 2006.

“Families are divided and separated,” said Mr. Abu Jamra, who works in logistics with the United Nations. “Why does someone who is not a criminal need forgiveness?”

Legal rights groups and some lawmakers argued the law should have included more explicit safeguards, such as excluding anyone who had served in the Israeli Army or committed war crimes in Lebanon, or requiring those who acquired Israeli citizenship to renounce it.

Some lawmakers also said the legislation had not been properly debated before a final vote. Others questioned whether it extended amnesty and sentence reductions beyond its intended beneficiaries.

Some lawmakers and legal rights groups even alleged that some wording in the bill had been altered by some lawmakers before it was sent to Mr. Aoun to sign.

Nizar Saghieh, co-founder of the Beirut-based advocacy group Legal Agenda, which monitors parliamentary proceedings, said the bill was changed after Parliament had voted, including modifications that removed or narrowed exclusions for certain corruption offenses. The changes come amid a broader fight over accountability for Lebanon’s 2019 banking collapse and lost deposits.

Lawmakers challenging the law before the Constitutional Council also said the text had been altered. These changes were “made in the dark,” Mr. Saghieh said. “This is destroying the rule of law.”

Mr. Aoun’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Paula Yacoubian, a lawmaker, said the signed law was “falsified” and could let major drug traffickers and corrupt officials go free.

“It’s disgraceful,” she said.

item.title: U.N. Seeks Relevance on A.I. as the U.S. and China Race Ahead
item.description:
As the threats posed by artificial intelligence spark international alarm, the stakes of the Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington this week have only grown bigger.

Earning considerably less attention are the meetings focused on A.I. at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, as world leaders gather in the shadow of several rogue A.I. hacking episodes that have prompted greater fears.

A.I. will be a dominant theme for a fleet of U.N. meetings on Monday centered on international digital cooperation. The schedule includes discussions about the technology’s risks and opportunities, the potential for economic dislocation and possible international governance.

Mr. Xi is expected to skip the General Assembly to instead convene in Washington with President Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed A.I. safety concerns as a hoax.

There is no shortage of tension between the two countries, and A.I. is just one of several issues the two sides are expected to discuss. But few issues are as contentious right now — or as important to humanity, some say — as the race for A.I. dominance.

The United States has repeatedly accused Chinese A.I. firms of stealing the intellectual property of American A.I. labs. China, too, continues to agitate against U.S. restrictions on advanced computer chips needed to power A.I. models.

Some onlookers, though expecting little, compared the urgency for a breakthrough on A.I. safety issues between the world’s two superpowers to the need for nuclear arms control agreements during the Cold War.

The U.N. gathering and the White House meeting underscore how much A.I. has become a race solely between two rival powers, with the rest of the world largely pushed to the periphery, foreign policy experts said.

“The U.N., to put it bluntly, has been sidelined in the A.I. conversation,” said Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies U.S.- China relations and focuses on technology issues.

A.I. is “a two-player game,” Mr. Chan added. “It’s kind of like nuclear weapons: If you do not have them or are not on the verge of having them, it’s hard to be relevant in shaping the discussion.”

Reflecting that reality, the United States and China discussed on Sunday creating a notification system to allow for the countries to alert each other about A.I.-driven national security risks. The mechanism, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, would be called “the U.S.-China A.I. dialogue.”

It is not for lack of trying. António Guterres, the U.N. secretary general, pushed last week for international cooperation on A.I., highlighting it as one of three existential risks facing humanity alongside climate change and deepening global inequality.

A.I., he said, presents other dangers, including amplifying misinformation, discrimination, privacy violations, cyberattacks and so-called superintelligence that could advance beyond human control.

“We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure and responsible development of A.I., while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require stronger safeguards,” Mr. Guterres said. “The world cannot afford a race to the bottom on A.I. safety.”

Under Mr. Guterres, the United Nations has been trying to build international consensus around responsible A.I. development for years, including by forming an advisory body in 2023 to study the issue. And on Monday, the leaders of 22 countries adopted a declaration calling to strengthen “human direction, oversight and control” of A.I. systems. The United States and China did not join the declaration.

The two countries have only further cemented their leads ahead of everyone else since the U.N. began worrying about A.I., rushing to build out data centers and release cutting-edge A.I. models despite growing fears about existential risks associated with the technology.

In his remarks last week, Mr. Guterres acknowledged that “geopolitical divides” made policing A.I. difficult but said that voluntary pauses on the technology would not work if not everyone agreed to them — meaning, right now, the United States and China.

China had generally been seeking to increase its influence with the United Nations, but this summer launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which has its headquarters in Shanghai, in a bid to assert global dominance on international A.I. discussions. The United States has shown little interest in building international consensus on A.I. or other geopolitical matters.

The U.N. Security Council may hold more sway on A.I. than the General Assembly. The OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman will speak to the Security Council on Wednesday, a company spokeswoman said. But it is difficult to imagine the Security Council — on which the United States, China and Russia sit — forging a consensus, experts said.

Mr. Altman’s appearance at the United Nations is just a warm-up. A day later in Washington, he will join a far larger roster of A.I. and technology leaders for the U.S.-China state dinner, including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, SpaceX’s Elon Musk and the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos.

Julian Ku, a professor of constitutional and international law at Hofstra University, said that the United Nations has always struggled to influence superpowers on the uses and limits of weapons they have that others do not, from nukes to high-powered hacking tools.

In the context of nuclear weapons, that took the form of helping nonnuclear nations gain access to nuclear power while spreading nonproliferation agreements, Mr. Ku said. While the United Nations would like to steer the A.I. safety conversation, it will probably find more success working to ensure the rest of the world is not fully left behind on the benefits societies could reap from the technology, Mr. Ku added.

“In a lot of ways, this is the story of the U.N. from the outset,” Mr. Ku said. “The U.N. can’t really shape the actions of those who have the power directly, but they do have the interests of everyone else who do not have that power.”

item.title: An Election Engineered to Send a Message That Putin’s Grip Remains Firm
item.description:
As near-final results came in on Monday for Russia’s first parliamentary elections since President Vladimir V. Putin invaded Ukraine, the Kremlin largely let the numbers do the talking. United Russia, the ruling party, was on track to win more seats than ever. Turnout, according to preliminary statistics, was the highest for a parliamentary vote in 15 years.

The elections were engineered in various ways to achieve the desired results, according to analysts, who cautioned that the numbers shouldn’t be read as an expression of how the Russian public feels. But they can be viewed for the message that the Kremlin was trying to send: Russia is rallying around Mr. Putin, who remains firmly in control despite the war’s challenges.

“The turnout categorically shows that the country supports the commander in chief, the country supports its army at war, and the country believes that we are acting justly, and that right is on our side,” Yevgeny Poddubny, a war correspondent for state television who ran as a United Russia candidate, said during a talk show on Sunday after voting had concluded.

It was a message designed for both domestic and international consumption, as the election authorities said United Russia had won as many as 355 of the 450 seats in the State Duma and claimed about 58 percent of the vote. That was higher than even state-run pollsters had projected.

Dmitri Kulikov, a pro-Kremlin commentator on state television, cheered the election result as a contribution to coming victory in the war. He called it a message to Western countries that he said were trying to destroy Russia by arming Ukraine.

“You know how they love to ‘send a message,’ right?” he said. “Well, we are sending them a very clear message: Don’t hold your breath. Better back off.”

While United Russia is a primary instrument of Mr. Putin’s power, he usually keeps a distance from the party, casting himself as an independent arbiter above politics. But this year, the party leaned in to its connection to Mr. Putin, who gave a clear endorsement at the party congress and was shown on camera with the party’s top candidates. In their ads, the candidates also leaned into the association with the president.

Mr. Putin, however, was publicly silent on Monday about the election results. The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said only that Mr. Putin would meet soon with the head of Russia’s election commission and the leaders of the parties that will enter the Duma, as the lower house of Parliament is known.

The election came just as Mr. Putin’s fortunes have begun to turn in the war, with Ukraine running short of air defenses and Russia employing new jet-powered drones. The U.S.-Israeli war in Iran has helped drive up the price of oil, one of Russia’s biggest exports, alleviating the challenge to Moscow’s finances posed by runaway war spending.

Still, Mr. Putin has struggled in recent months with rising discontent over declining economic prospects, widening internet restrictions and increasing Ukrainian drone and missile strikes. That prompted questions about whether those feelings would somehow show up in the election results.

But the vote, as expected, was a highly stage-managed affair, limited to approved parties, with some people forced to cast ballots. Russia also has strict laws on demonstrating against or criticizing the war, and it has ensured that antiwar figures remaining in the country continue to face pressure from the authorities.

In August, Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko, the only party running on an antiwar platform, from appearing on the ballot, as polls showed the party gaining in popularity and possibly poised to win enough votes to enter Parliament.

Some of the party’s candidates were able to stay on the ballot in their individual districts, but none won. The party did meet the threshold to get into the regional legislature in Novgorod, near St. Petersburg. That region was the only one that allowed the party on the ballot in a regional election.

The party’s chairman, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrated his contempt for what he described as an unfair election by depositing a ballot at his polling station with the words “For freedom yes Yabloko” written across the text in green marker. Eight Yabloko members are in prison for expressing antiwar views, including Lev Shlosberg, who was sentenced to 11 years for “discrediting the Russian military.”

To a large degree, the election demonstrated that Mr. Putin’s autocratic system was still functioning and able to deliver the result he sought, despite a small element of unpredictability from the rising discontent, said Tatiana Stanovaya, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

“There was a certain margin — not a very large one — that created a risk of things potentially going wrong,” Ms. Stanovaya said. “The question was whether the system and the regime were strong and stable enough to deliver the results Putin wanted to see, despite these new risks.”

She said the system had proved its ability “to control the situation without any surprises, despite the rising antiwar sentiment, despite anxiety and the decline in the approval ratings of the authorities.”

Mr. Putin’s government repeatedly emphasized that Russia was carrying out the election despite difficult circumstances, an implicit criticism of Ukraine, which by law cannot hold elections under martial law.

Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said on Sunday that Ukraine had carried out the biggest attack of the war on the Russian capital on the last of three days of voting. The city’s largest oil refinery, which Ukraine hit earlier in the year, was struck again. The Russian authorities also asserted that the election had withstood cyberattacks from several countries, including Ukraine.

Ms. Stanovaya said that while the election results had not been an accurate reflection of Russian popular opinion, the voting did confirm that Mr. Putin continued to have a base of support, albeit not as big as the authorities claimed.

“Of course, United Russia doesn’t have 57 percent, but it doesn’t have 10 percent, either,” Ms. Stanovaya said. “A significant portion of the population did, after all, vote for the ruling party.”

Oleg Matsnev contributed reporting.

item.title: A Power Shift in America?
item.description:
When President Trump won a second term, he didn’t just win the presidency. The Republican Party he leads also retook the Senate and kept control of the House of Representatives. This control of both the executive and the legislative branches has given him a pretty free hand to do what he wants without meaningful pushback. Like start a trade war. And a real war.

But in six weeks, that could change. That’s when the United States holds midterm elections. All the seats in the House and a third of the seats in the Senate are up for grabs. My colleague Nate Cohn, our polling wizard at The New York Times, has looked at all the data points and says that, on paper at least, the Democrats have a real chance of winning big.

By Nate Cohn

Last week, a new New York Times/Siena poll found that the conditions for a so-called wave in November’s midterm elections might be coming into place. The only question is whether Democrats will be able to ride it.

Overall, Democrats lead Republicans, 51 percent to 43 percent, among likely voters asked which party they will support for Congress in their district.

That’s “blue wave” territory. At least in terms of the national vote, the Democratic margin in the poll — 8.5 points — would almost exactly match the party’s 8.6-point margin in 2018, when the Democrats regained control of the House of Representatives in Trump’s first term. And it would exceed the winning margins for the party out of power in other recent wave elections, like in 1994, 2006 and 2010.

The Times/Siena poll is just one survey, and polls are imprecise and subject to many sources of potential error. But this is also far from the only data point showing a major Democratic advantage.

The results are almost exactly in line with the average of other polls. And it’s not just the polls. The results of recent special elections also point to Democrats going into the midterms with momentum behind them. So, for that matter, does the long history of midterm elections going back to the dawn of party politics; they tend to favor the party out of power.

But whether Democrats can translate these enormous national advantages into control of the Senate and a significant House majority — which would give Democrats more oversight power and, in the case of the Senate, leverage over Trump’s nominations — is a more complicated question.

The George W. Bush example

Winning control of the House, where every seat will be up for election, is easier than winning control of the Senate, where only one-third of seats are up for grabs in any election year. To win the Senate, Democrats will need to win at least two seats where Trump won by at least 11 points in the last election. That’s really tough, even in a wave year.

The 2006 midterms offer a useful comparison.

As my colleague Carl Hulse recently pointed out, there are a lot of similarities between Trump’s predicament today and George W. Bush’s that year. Both presidents were unpopular: Trump’s approval rating is just 38 percent among likely voters; Bush’s was about the same. Bush was in a quagmire in Iraq and dogged by high gas prices. Today, Trump has just a 31 percent approval rating on the war in Iran and a 28 percent rating on the cost of living.

Even so, to flip the Senate in 2006, Democrats needed to win at least a few seats in states where Bush had won by at least eight points in the previous election. In the end, they pulled it off — but only barely, including two extremely narrow victories of less than one point in Montana and Virginia. Without a few fortunate breaks, those races could have gone the other way, along with the Senate. The result would have been less aggressive oversight of the Iraq war, among other differences.

The national environment may have been great for Democrats, but a Senate win was far from inevitable.

Too far to the left?

With Trump’s approval ratings so far underwater, Republicans may have only one realistic card to play: try to rally their base and hold on to Republican-leaning independents by casting the Democrats as too far to the left.

Republicans didn’t have a similar opportunity in 2006, when Democrats assiduously nominated moderate candidates in key red states and districts. While Democrats have nominated candidates with broad appeal in most states this year, there are at least a few competitive races — most notably the Senate contest in Michigan — where Democrats have nominated candidates far to the left of anything the party would have contemplated 20 years ago. They’ve also nominated left-wing candidates in a number of noncompetitive races, which has driven considerable national media coverage of the party’s lurch to the left.

The poll does contain hints that primary victories this summer by progressive and democratic socialist candidates have made the Democratic Party less palatable to some voters. About half of voters — 50 percent of likely voters — say the party is “too far” to the left. That’s up from 46 percent in the last Times/Siena poll of registered voters in May, which was conducted before the democratic socialist surge in New York, Colorado and beyond.

But it’s also hard to see any sign it’s damaging Democrats in the survey results — and in particular, in any question that pits Democrats against Republicans. Voters say, for instance, that Republicans are more extreme than Democrats by an eight-point margin, 48-40.

And at a time when Republicans hold the White House and Congress, voters will tend to be much more concerned about Republican excesses than Democratic ones. That’s part of what makes midterm elections so hard for the party in power.

item.title: With Time on His Side, Xi Seeks to Extend Truce With Trump
item.description:
When China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, and President Trump meet in Washington this week, the two men will be operating on vastly different clocks.

The American president is constrained by the immediate demands of a midterm election in November and a grinding war. The Chinese leader is gearing up for a norm-shattering fourth term as head of the ruling Communist Party, that will keep him in power for another five years.

For Mr. Xi, the disparity in political realities gives him an edge in maintaining the truce that the two countries reached last year. A renewed trade fight would hit American consumers right before the election — a risk Mr. Trump can ill afford. China’s economy is struggling too, but Mr. Xi answers to no electorate, giving him the patience to prolong the détente on his terms.

“Each of Xi’s face-to-face encounters with Trump in his second term would only have reinforced Xi’s prior conviction that Trump is leading an America that is dangerous but declining,” said Jonathan Czin, a researcher at the Brookings Institution who previously worked at the C.I.A. analyzing Chinese politics.

Mr. Xi, who will sit down for talks with Mr. Trump on Thursday, may be wagering that leaning into Mr. Trump’s preference for leader-to-leader diplomacy can insulate the relationship from flash points like the status of Taiwan, the self-governed island claimed by Beijing, and the competition to dominate artificial intelligence.

Keeping Mr. Trump at bay would give Mr. Xi breathing room to work on rejuvenating his listless economy, which has been weakened by a property crisis, high youth unemployment and excess production. It would give him time to rebuild the upper echelons of his military leadership, which he has hollowed out in a drive against corruption and disloyalty. And it would allow him to continue expanding his country’s industrial, technological and military strength for a future showdown with the United States.

Analysts say China benefits every time Mr. Trump’s attention drifts elsewhere. By quarreling with traditional American allies or sinking deeper into the war in Iran, Mr. Trump is weakening his country's global standing and pulling troops away from the Pacific.

“Xi would love to tell Trump, ‘Go on, stay the course,’” said Suisheng Zhao, executive director of the China Center at the University of Denver. “For Xi, Trump represents a window of opportunity for China, so his priority is to buy more time.”

Since first meeting Mr. Trump at Mar-a-Lago more than nine years ago — a gathering best remembered for being when Mr. Xi learned about U.S. missile strikes on Syria while dining on what Mr. Trump described as the “most beautiful chocolate cake” — Mr. Xi has had an extraordinary amount of time for a Chinese leader to size up his chief geopolitical rival.

Early in Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Xi was somewhat accommodating toward the American president. In 2018, his government agreed to purchase $200 billion in additional U.S. goods and services to offset a trade imbalance (though Beijing never fully honored that deal.)

Last year, Mr. Xi flipped the dynamic between the two superpowers.

Faced with Mr. Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, Mr. Xi was the only world leader who refused to back down, choosing instead to match his opponent with one sky-high tariff after another. Mr. Xi then reached for his ace card by throttling exports of Chinese critical minerals, or rare earths, which companies globally need for modern technologies. Backed into a corner, the Trump administration called for a truce.

It was a payoff years in the making: a rare instance in which Beijing not only withstood U.S. pressure but turned the tables and forced it to relent. Beijing, as a result, is emboldened today and sees itself more as an equal to Washington, analysts say.

The Trump administration “thought they could use massive unilateral pressure to force China to make concessions. And that did not occur. In fact, the opposite did,” said Scott Kennedy, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

“I think now this is Xi Jinping’s world and we’re all living in it,” he added.

The superpowers should put limits on competition, Mr. Xi’s argument goes, to avoid what he has warned could be a catastrophic clash. To this end, he has pushed a formula he calls “constructive strategic stability.”

In practice, what this means is that Beijing wants Washington to accept boundaries on where it can challenge China.

In July, for example, when the U.S. Federal Communications Commission proposed a ban on Chinese-made humanoid robots, China’s Ministry of Commerce invoked the phrase, demanding that Washington roll back the restrictions to preserve “strategic stability.”

American analysts view the slogan not as a serious effort at ironing out differences but as an attempt to get Washington to recognize China’s clout and back off. China could apply it to any new U.S. restrictions on chip exports or arms sales to Taiwan.

“The truce is not constructive because little diplomatic infrastructure is being built,” Mr. Czin of the Brookings Institution said. “It is tactical rather than strategic. And therefore it is inherently unstable.”

Mr. Xi appears to have calculated that the best way to manage the United States is to engage Mr. Trump in high-profile summits rich in optics but thin in substance.

The planned meeting on Thursday will be their third face-to-face in less than a year, a pace that could continue with talks in November at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and at the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

“Head-of-state diplomacy is the cornerstone of China-U.S. relations,” China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, told Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a call on Thursday.

But beyond extending the trade truce, the meetings have produced few breakthroughs. China may agree to more agricultural purchases this week, but expectations are low on issues like A.I. safety or China’s trade imbalances.

That is by design, analysts say. Enticing Mr. Trump with the pageantry of summits he seems to relish lowers the risk that he may do something to derail relations — like greenlight a package of arms to Taiwan.

Tellingly, Mr. Trump has avoided criticizing China in the lead-up to the talks, even downplaying a Wall Street Journal report that China had supplied Iran with satellite images of a U.S. base in Jordan where three American troops were killed in an Iranian strike.

The summitry will also serve a domestic purpose for Mr. Xi by burnishing his image at home as a global statesman, during a moment of economic anxiety for many Chinese. It is important for Mr. Xi to demonstrate that he can manage Beijing’s most critical bilateral relationship, analysts say.

Mr. Trump is expected to greet Mr. Xi personally on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland when his plane lands on Wednesday. The White House will host Mr. Xi and Peng Liyuan, the first lady, for a state dinner, the first such banquet since King Charles III and Queen Camilla visited in April.

“Xi wants to be seen by the Chinese public as a highly respected, influential and consequential world leader — and nothing can top being wined and dined at the White House,” said Minxin Pei, a professor at Claremont McKenna College who studies Chinese leadership politics.

“Xi cannot afford to be distracted by a huge confrontation with the United States,” Mr. Pei said.

Berry Wang contributed research.

item.title: Trump’s U.N. Speech Comes at a Time of Tumult
item.description:
President Trump will address global leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday morning as he is confronted with a deeply unpopular war in Iran, rising concerns about the unpredictability of artificial intelligence and allies that have begun to openly question whether the United States remains a credible partner.

In addition to a series of global crises, Mr. Trump is also juggling a packed schedule. After delivering his address, the president is expected to meet with leaders of Britain, Japan, Venezuela and a number of Persian Gulf nations.

He is also expected to sign an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that Mr. Trump says will expand the U.S. security presence in the semiautonomous Danish territory, according to a White House official speaking on the condition of anonymity to preview the schedule. The signing comes after Mr. Trump this year demanded total control of Greenland, a threat that prompted intense criticism from allies who will be at the opening of the United Nations session in New York.

Mr. Trump will again face a United Nations that he has long derided as outdated, inefficient and beholden to powers that revel in defying American wishes. But this year, more than most, he is increasingly isolated on the world stage. Here are some of the more pressing issues he will encounter at the 81st session of the General Assembly.

Mr. Trump enters the summit with a track record of attacking, rather than uniting, many of the attendees.

When he first attended the gathering as president in 2017, Mr. Trump was largely subdued. That was not the case last year, when he questioned whether the U.N should exist, lectured the world leaders about their immigration policies and bashed allies and foes across the globe. “Your countries are going to hell,” Mr. Trump said.

But that was before his biggest international gamble yet — starting a war with Iran that he was convinced would topple its 47-year-old leadership — went south. He makes no secret of his anger at allies who refused to help open the Strait of Hormuz and who declared that his war was illegal.

The president may be the odd man out even more so this time around. He has attacked many European leaders for not supporting the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran. His threats to take over Greenland nearly upended the Western alliance and in part prompted Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada to warn of a “rupture” in the world order. The United States and Canada are still locked in a trade war.

Mr. Trump met with France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, at Trump Tower on Monday, and it remains to be seen how Mr. Trump will approach his first meeting with Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham. But the introduction will come after Mr. Trump weighed in on a highly divisive subject this month by endorsing the unification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, which is still part of the United Kingdom. That came just days after Mr. Burnham had said reunification was off the table for now.

Mr. Trump will join members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the U.S. allies Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman. The nations in the Gulf region are likely to raise concerns about the soaring energy prices caused by the fallout of the war in Iran, which has shown little sign of ending.

Mr. Trump will argue in his speech that the war in Iran is necessary to prevent the nation from having a nuclear weapon, according to a U.S. official speaking on the condition of anonymity to preview the summit. That message has not helped quell worries among Americans over the war in Iran, its disruption of supply chains and the fueling of economic anxiety.

In addition to the conflict in Iran, Mr. Trump must also decide whether he should aid the Saudis in their fight against the Iranian-backed Houthis. Mr. Trump so far has resisted the Saudi Arabia’s appeals to have the United States launch strikes in Yemen.

The threat posed by artificial intelligence has jumped to the top of the U.N. agenda, after a summer of surprises, including A.I. agents that broke out of the “sandboxes” where they were being tested, conducted cyberattacks on their own and covered their tracks. Now Mr. Trump, while dismissing potential serious threats as a “HOAX” and deflecting calls for him to impose guardrails on the new technology, is trying to figure out the value of slowing down Chinese progress, as well. He has said that efforts to rein in A.I. amount to a “sick conspiracy.”

Some officials in the Trump administration are urging caution in embracing artificial intelligence, particularly after some A.I. agents went rogue. But Mr. Trump’s anti-regulatory stance is also fueled by influential Silicon Valley voices like David Sacks, the venture capitalist who interceded to weaken an executive order in May that would have required safety reviews of new A.I. models; Mark Zuckerberg of Meta; and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

Mr. Trump will have his first in-person meeting with Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela’s new leader after the United States deposed and captured Nicolás Maduro, who is imprisoned just across the East River in Brooklyn.

Ms. Rodríguez has gained favor with Mr. Trump since the military operation, particularly by allowing the United States to expand its access and control over Venezuela’s oil reserves. Mr. Trump last month announced a deal to take majority control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves, as he hopes to assert dominance over energy in the Western Hemisphere.

item.title: ‘My Husband Is in Love With His Valet’: Takeaways From Charles Spencer’s Memoir
item.description:
“Swan Song” weaves Charles Spencer’s early memories of Princess Diana with the planning and execution of her funeral service. In the introduction, Spencer says that “the aim of the book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective,” just as he did during her fiery eulogy. With the 30th anniversary of her death looming, he writes, “I thought, You know what? … I am going to tell things how I remember them, lay them down for good, once and for all.”

Spencer, younger than Diana by three years, tells many affecting tales of his sister’s bravery. The one that stands out is the day the two of them, along with their mother, were checking their lobster pots off the coast of Scotland when one of them yielded a nasty surprise: a “lithe, black, muscular conger eel, which was around four feet long and as thick as my arm,” Spencer writes. As it thrashed about their boat, gnashing its sharp teeth, he and his mother cowered while Diana grabbed a penknife “and brought its point down hard behind the eel’s eyes.” (Spencer considered telling this story at Diana’s funeral but thought better of it.)

Spencer writes that Diana, who was 7 when their parents divorced, discovered that their father had married Raine, the former Countess of Dartmouth — whom the children all detested — by reading an article in the newspaper. “Diana was so disappointed and outraged by my father’s secret marriage that she slapped him across the face — the only time she physically clashed with either parent,” Spencer writes, “while saying, on behalf of Sarah, Jane and me, ‘That’s for the pain you’re causing us all.’”

Not long after she began dating Prince Charles, Diana, 19, showed up at Eton — as she often did — to take her little brother to lunch. Spencer writes that he caught sight of her red Mini Metro from his window with “a dozen strange cars and a motorbike in tow. … Diana parked carefully outside my house, while the strangers’ vehicles slewed to a halt haphazardly in the middle of the street, their ignitions still on, disgorging men — some alone, others in pairs — who converged on her like hyenas closing in on a gazelle.”

According to Spencer, shortly after their engagement, Prince Charles squeezed Diana’s waist and said, “Oh, a bit chubby here, aren’t we?” Spencer also writes that he learned from a friend of Diana’s that, the day before their wedding, Prince Charles told her “that she needed to know that he was very happy to marry her, but he was not actually in love with her.” Later, Spencer writes, he was visiting his sister at Kensington Palace when the thump of her disco music led Prince Charles to scream, “Get her to turn off that infernal racket!”

When Spencer’s father, the Earl of Spencer, died in 1992, Prince Charles came to Althorp with Diana for the funeral. According to Spencer, the prince said to him, “You’re just so lucky — you know, inheriting when you’re so young!” He added, “I’m 43, and I employ 50 people … but my parents insist on treating me like — like a child!”

During a tea at Althorp, the Spencers’ ancestral family home, their stepmother Raine was rude to their mother, Frances Shand Kydd. “When Diana discovered this, she confronted Raine with incredulity. … ‘Do you really have no idea how to behave?’” Raine shot back, “I have always felt so very sorry for the Prince of Wales, marrying someone quite as stupid as you.” Spencer writes that “Diana paused for a second, surprised at the intensity of the spite. She then took a step forward, hooked a long leg round Raine’s calves before shoving her down the carpeted staircase.”

Spencer writes that over lunch at her favorite London restaurant, Diana told him, “I’m going to get divorced,” adding, “My husband is in love with his valet.” Diana, Spencer says, “did not name the member of staff, and I never asked her who it was, or why she would believe such an improbable thing. It was not important: The end of her marriage, and of her dreams, was.”

Spencer is frank about the ups and downs of his relationship with his sister. “The astonishing pressures of her life, and her reactive nature, saw her fall out with each of us regularly,” Spencer writes. “She was on non-speaks with two of our closest relatives for months before her death, over not very much at all.”

When Spencer learned that the palace had extended funeral invitations to Fleet Street editors, he placed calls to all of them, asking them to stay home. “They were unable to be rude to the brother of the much-mourned princess and, although clearly highly surprised by my call, they each agreed not to come,” Spencer writes. “The only one who sounded surly, as opposed to merely confused or embarrassed, was Piers Morgan of The Mirror, who snarled with annoyance before he hung up.”

At the rehearsal the day before the funeral, Spencer realized with a start that he had, in effect, walked into an ambush, that the assembled courtiers were there to vet his eulogy. Bluffing his way out of the situation, he told them: “God, I’m stupid! … In all the excitement of getting here on time, I’ve only gone and left my speech at home!”

When Diana’s service at Westminster Abbey concluded, Spencer writes, he got on the royal train headed back to Althorp for her burial, where his brother-in-law Robert Fellowes — Queen Elizabeth’s private secretary — told him that the monarch, who had stripped Diana of her royal titles after the divorce, had offered to reinstate them. Spencer replied: “That’s very kind of the queen, of course. But what’s the point, Robert? Now? I mean — Diana’s dead.”

item.title: A Brotherly Tribute to the People’s Princess, No Holds Barred
item.description:
SWAN SONG: Diana, My Sister, by Charles Spencer

Delivering a eulogy is hard enough. Now imagine delivering one to around 2.5 billion people.

This was the surreal task that fell to Charles Spencer, younger brother of Diana, the Princess of Walesafter she died following a car crash at 36 in the summer of 1997. Her driver, who had been trying to evade paparazzi, died at the scene, along with her boyfriend, Dodi Fayed.

In a speech that was beamed from Westminster Abbey, Spencer chastised the press whose pursuit led to Diana’s demise and sideswiped the royal family that had, among other indignities, stripped her of her title. “A girl given the name of the ancient goddess of hunting,” he noted, “was, in the end, the most hunted person of the modern age.”

The applause that followed began outside, among the hoi polloi whose adoration led to her anointment as the People’s Princess. Scattered at first, the clapping began to spread, becoming a wall of sound that rolled into the abbey, up to the vaulted ceilings, and through living rooms around the world.

Now, almost 30 years later, comes the coda: Spencer’s elegant and reproving new memoir, “Swan Song.” In between, with a degree in history from Oxford, he became a part-time journalist and wrote nine books of nonfiction, as if to model a standard of truth-telling disregarded in the “coverage” of his sister.

Save to your reading list:

Neither of Spencer’s parents lived past 70, and at 62 he feels a sense of if-not-now-when. “This is the work that really matters to me,” he writes.

The title alludes not only to his own fatalism, but to Diana’s favorite black swans from a board game that they played as children. A lament of them now circle the island where she is buried.

“Swan Song” is most compelling as a postcard from the siblings’ nursery, where their bond was solidified after their parents’ marriage dissolved in the late 1960s. (Two older sisters, Sarah and Jane, had already left the house.) He called her “Duch.” She called him “Carlos.” He still remembers “the squeak of our descent” as they slid, against the house rules, down the well-polished wooden banister of Park House.

Theirs was an upbringing typical of upper-class families, of well-appointed neglect. There were good nannies and very bad nannies, one of whom bashed their heads together or against a concrete wall. Spencer wrote about further abuse in his 2024 memoir, “A Very Private School” (as used to be customary for his class, he was sent off, miserable, at the age of 8). But contrary to reports, he writes, his father, John, the eighth Earl of Spencer, was a gentle if traditional and parsimonious soul: hiring a camel named Bert for Diana’s 7th birthday party and taking them for ice-cream outings on Brancaster beach.

Their parents’ marriage was frayed inexorably by the death of their first son, born with a hole in the back of his head and other malformations, possibly due to a Thalidomide-like medication. The children’s mother, Frances, left John for Peter Shand Kydd after falling in love with him on a ski trip, leaving Diana, who supposed herself a disappointing third daughter, permanently bereft and taking on a maternal role herself, drawing curtains against the dark at night and checking up on her “Carlos” in nursery school.

Contrary to the shy lip-biter portrayed on “The Crown,” Diana is in Spencer’s telling fierce and athletic, diving off a high slide into the family’s pool and once pushing their loathed stepmother, Raine, down a carpeted staircase like a character in “Dynasty.” On one lobster-potting trip, as others cowered, Diana killed a four-foot-long conger eel with a swift penknife blow behind the eyes.

With his pen, her brother likewise delivers a series of lacerations to his former in-laws. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, exiled from the princehood after his association with the sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein, is spotted smirking as a teen after a priest refers to “the Virgin’s womb.” Princess Anne comes off as just rude, batting away his teenage attempts at small talk. Prince Charles gets mingy when Diana tries to give her brother some unused household items bearing their shared name, then later angles to be at the center of his ex-wife’s two-mile funeral procession. (He did not prevail.) “Rest assured,” he hisses to Spencer during their discussion of funeral arrangements. “We’ll forget her soon enough.”

Yeah … no.

Even with all its bitterness toward bad actors, like the deceptive Diana interviewer Martin Bashir, this is a lyrical book that delights in moments of the British absurd. One member of Prince Charles’s retinue bleats “I am a tree!,” Monty Pythonishly, as he tries to blend in during Diana’s burial. Elsewhere, Spencer seems to relish in the chambermaids’ helplessly evocative names — Violet Collison? — and remembers thinking his mother was declaring herself “going potty,” as in crazy, when in fact she was just announcing a visit to the loo.

This is the work of a man who is resigned but has not given up.

SWAN SONG: Diana, My Sister | By Charles Spencer | Penguin Press | 384 pp. | $35

item.title: Typhoon Dujuan Brings Record Rain to Japan, Killing 5 People
item.description:
Five people have died as Typhoon Dujuan battered Japan with heavy rain, dumping more than 20 inches on one island and prompting evacuation advisories for the threat of flooding and landslides, the authorities said on Tuesday.

The storm had moved northeast away from Japan as of Tuesday morning, the Japan Meteorological Agency said. Still, more than 74,000 people were under evacuation instructions, largely in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo, according to a Tuesday afternoon update from Japan’s Fire and Disaster Management Agency. Earlier, the number of affected residents had been over 500,000.

One person was killed in a landslide in Sammu, a city in Chiba, according to the agency. It did not specify the cause of the four other deaths, two of which were also in Chiba.

Six people were missing as of noon Tuesday, the agency said.

The storm brought record rainfall to parts of Japan’s Pacific coast. Oshima, an island south of Tokyo, received 27 inches of rain over 24 hours on Monday, a September record, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency. A landslide warning for the island was fully lifted on Tuesday morning, municipal officials said, after the agency issued its highest alert on Monday.

This year, the El Niño phenomenon, which develops when Pacific Ocean waters become unusually warm, has contributed to stronger storms and more extreme weather. El Niño scrambles weather patterns, suppressing rainfall and fanning wildfires in some parts of the world while bringing heavy rains, floods and landslides to others.

Videos from Monday showed pedestrians and vehicles in Tokyo and Chiba prefecture moving through deep water on sidewalks and roads. Several train lines remained suspended or delayed on Tuesday because of the typhoon, according to the East Japan Railway Company.

At Haneda, Tokyo’s busiest airport, nearly 400 flights were canceled on Monday, according to the aviation tracking website FlightAware. Narita Airport, the larger international hub in Chiba prefecture, saw more than 100 flights canceled, according to FlightAware.

The storm also delayed Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s departure for New York on Monday night to attend the opening of the United Nations General Assembly.

Several major international events in Japan were also disrupted.

Rock in Japan, an annual music festival, canceled the final day of the festival on Monday, while the Tokyo Game Show, one of the world’s biggest video game conventions, ended a day early because of the storm.

The agency had forecast up to 13 inches of rain in Japan’s central Tokai region, which includes the city of Nagoya. The Asian Games, which are being held in the city, postponed an equestrian competition until Tuesday, according to its website.

item.title: What to Know About the United Nations and the General Assembly
item.description:
For more than eight decades, the United Nations has tried to bring countries together to address global poverty, provide humanitarian aid, resolve armed conflicts and make the world more peaceful.

Here is a look at its history and the role of the annual U.N. General Assembly, which convenes this week with nearly 200 leaders.

The United Nations Charter was signed at a conference in San Francisco in June 1945, led by Britain, China, the Soviet Union and the United States.

When the Charter took effect on Oct. 24 that year, a devastating global war had just ended, leaving millions dead and much of the industrialized world in ruins. Many parts of Africa and Asia were still ruled by colonial powers, which had been weakened in the war.

After fierce negotiations, 50 nations agreed to a Charter that begins, “We the peoples of the United Nations.”

That opening line is notable, critics say, because today the United Nations can sometimes seem to serve the national interests of the most powerful among its 193 members. Their priorities often stand in the way of fulfilling the Charter’s first two pledges: to end “the scourge of war” and to regain “faith in fundamental human rights.”

The General Assembly is the main decision-making body of the United Nations. The gathering takes place for a week every fall, when presidents and prime ministers deliver speeches that can be soaring, clichéd or somewhere in between.

Many leaders exceed the recommended 15-minute time limit. Some have delivered long, incoherent tirades. (In September 1960, the Cuban leader Fidel Castro gave the longest General Assembly speech on record: four hours and 29 minutes.)

Secretary General António Guterres, whose term concludes at the end of the year, is expected to deliver his final address to the gathering this week. Mr. Guterres has led the U.N. through wars, financial challenges and changes to the U.N. system, all while navigating a tense relationship with President Trump.

Some of the most closely watched speeches this year will be those by Mr. Trump; President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran; leaders of Arab countries in the Persian Gulf; President Emmanuel Macron of France; President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine; Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel; and the Palestinian leader, Mahmoud Abbas, who will deliver a speech by video because the United States denied him a visa.

The speeches usually offer insight into the priorities and worldview of the speaker. In the past, however, they have seldom done much to resolve conflicts or make progress on major global challenges like climate change and food insecurity.

Last year, for instance, Mr. Trump offered a meandering address in which he rebuked global institutions and complained about immigration, environmentalists and windmills.

Aside from the speeches, hundreds of resolutions are generally voted on each year by the General Assembly, with each country having one vote. The resolutions are not legally binding, so their power is mostly symbolic. Still, some past resolutions have earned much attention, such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, one on granting independence to colonial countries in 1960 and another that equated Zionism with racism in 1975.

In principle, nations large and small have an equal voice in the Assembly, but the real power lies with the 15-member U.N. Security Council, and especially its five permanent members.

The Council can authorize military intervention, as it did against Libya in 2011 and in Haiti in 2023. It can also impose sanctions on states, and it has done so against North Korea over its nuclear arsenal, against Sudan because of its civil war and against Iran for its nuclear program.

Critics say the panel is often paralyzed by its anachronistic structure. Its five permanent members, known as the P5, are the victors of World War II: Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States. The other 10 members are elected for two-year terms, with seats set aside for different regions of the world.

Any member of the P5 can veto any measure, and each has regularly wielded this power to protect itself or allies. The United States has vetoed 95 Council resolutions, many concerning Israeli-Palestinian relations. It has used its veto repeatedly since a Hamas-led attack on Israel in October 2023 set off a brutal war in Gaza.

The Soviet Union and its successor, Russia, has logged even more vetoes over the years, though most were before the end of the Cold War. China has used the veto power the least, but in the past two decades, many of those vetoes have aligned with Russian interests.

Efforts to expand the P5 to include powers that have emerged since 1945 — like India, Japan or Germany — have been stymied. Whenever a country vies for a permanent seat, rivals seek to block it.

item.title: Trump Set to Sign Deal on U.S. Presence in Greenland
item.description:
The United States was set on Tuesday to sign an agreement about Greenland, the Arctic island that has been one of President Trump’s obsessions.

Mr. Trump said last week that after months of negotiations between the United States, Denmark and Greenland, a semiautonomous Danish territory, his administration had reached a deal to expand the U.S. security presence on the island.

He is expected to sign the agreement with the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland in New York, where world leaders are gathering for the U.N. General Assembly meeting.

The hope on all sides is that the agreement will end more than a year of tensions that were sparked by Mr. Trump’s threats to seize the island and that caused a rift in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.

Details of the deal have remained a mystery. Mr. Trump claimed last week that the United States had secured “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland, while the Danish prime minister said the deal “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity” of the Kingdom of Denmark. The agreement appears to fall far short of Mr. Trump’s longstanding demands to take over the island, which he has said is essential to American security.

Negotiators have been working for months on issues including the deployment of more American troops in Greenland, the territory’s mineral resources and ways of blocking Russia and China from gaining a foothold there. Russia and China have been stepping up their presence in the Arctic, sometimes working together, which Mr. Trump has used to justify his desire to annex Greenland.

Many analysts have wondered how Tuesday’s deal would differ from a decades-old defense agreement that grants American forces sweeping access to Greenland.

That agreement, signed in 1951, allows the United States to “construct, install, maintain, and operate” military bases across the territory, as well as to house personnel and “control landings, takeoffs, anchorages, moorings, movements, and operation of ships, aircraft, and waterborne craft.” Greenland is already NATO territory as a part of Denmark, one of the alliance’s founding members.

The island is bigger than Mexico but sparsely populated. Many of its 57,000 or so residents have voiced concerns about the new agreement, saying they don’t want a larger U.S. military presence.

item.title: Iran’s President Travels to U.S. Against Backdrop of War

With the United States and Iran locked in a dragging conflict, President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran was traveling to New York on Tuesday to attend the annual meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.

It will be the first instance of a leader whose country is at war with the United States setting foot on U.S. soil in recent decades. Just before departing Iran, Mr. Pezeshkian had referred to his host country for the next few days as the “enemy” in combative remarks carried by state media.

“They cannot use force to compel people to submit,” he said of the United States, accusing it of repeatedly violating truce agreements and using its military to strike homes and hospitals and “commit atrocities” in Iran and beyond.

Mr. Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. gathering on Wednesday, speaking after President Evariste Ndayishimiye of Burundi and before President Santiago Peña of Paraguay.

The State Department said last week that as the host country, the United States had permitted Iran to send a core delegation to attend the U.N.’s largest annual meeting.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was among those granted a visa. In a statement posted on social media on Tuesday, he said he was in New York to shore up support on the world stage despite the “state of war” between the United States and Iran.

As well as meeting with other world leaders, Mr. Pezeshkian would meet with “intellectuals, members of the media and Iranian and non-Iranian scholars” during his time in New York, Mr. Araghchi said. The State Department typically restricts the movements of the Iranian delegation, prohibiting its members from traveling without permission beyond a limited area of Midtown Manhattan, where the U.N. headquarters are located.

item.title: U.N. Leader Uses Final Speech to Issue Stark Warning
item.description:
António Guterres, the secretary general of the United Nations, delivered his final address to the General Assembly in New York on Tuesday morning, laying out the perils the world faces and urging leaders to reverse course before it was too late.

Mr. Guterres, 77, issued a blunt assessment of the state of global affairs, warning of the need to deal with urgent challenges at a time when the divisions between nations only seem to be growing.

“The faultlines in our world are widening,” he said. “Cracks have become canyons.”

“Looking ahead, our future will be shaped by how we address four great tests of power,” he added. “The power over war and peace. The power that concentrates wealth and drives inequality. The power fueling climate chaos and the war on nature. And the power unleashed by artificial intelligence.”

Senior U.N. diplomats said Mr. Guterres, who steps down at the end of his second term in December, wanted to deliver a goodbye speech that focused on the future and not his own legacy. He has presided over the U.N. since 2017, a turbulent era marked by wars in Ukraine, Gaza, Iran and elsewhere, and natural disasters on a grand scale.

Mr. Guterres said the events of this year in particular had demonstrated that even the strongest nations had their limits, and that building a better future “begins with a recognition, especially by superpowers, that their power isn’t so super.”

He also repeated a plea that he has made every year, urging world leaders to collaborate and adhere to the framework of the U.N. Charter to uphold international law, multilateralism and respect for human rights.

“There is another path,” Mr. Guterres said. “A networked world recognizes that no power can solve today’s challenges alone.” He added that the very creation of the U.N. after World War II was an act of hopeful defiance against humanity’s history of warfare by “countries that know our futures are bound together.”

His time at the helm of the U.N. also coincided with President Trump’s two terms in office, which he had to carefully navigate because the United States is not only the host of the United Nations headquarters but also its top donor. While Mr. Trump has said he values the U.N., he has said is losing relevance, withdrawn from U.N. agencies and defunded U.N.-run humanitarian programs.

During his speech, Mr. Guterres continued to walk a verbal tightrope by avoiding statements that could anger Mr. Trump.

Mr. Guterres called out Russia by name for invading Ukraine and causing human suffering by disrupting global food and energy supply chains with its war. But he made no direct mention of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran and the turmoil and civilian casualties that it has caused.

Instead, he spoke only in broad terms of unspecified regional confrontations.

“Across the Middle East, conflicts are cascading,” Mr. Guterres said. “Enough is enough.” He called for all nations involved to return to diplomacy.

Mr. Guterres also talked at length about combating climate change and strengthening governance of A.I. Warning that the impacts of global warming fall disproportionately on poorer nations, he called on all governments to adopt plans to transition away from fossil fuels “with clear timelines and protection for affected workers and communities.”

“As tragic events have shown — impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder and spreading further than many anticipated,” Mr. Guterres said.

He said the nations leading the way in A.I. bore the greatest responsibility for mitigating its risks, urging the great powers to work together just as they did after World War II.

“Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks,” Mr. Guterres said. “Cooperate on testing and evaluation. And work toward common safeguards that protect us all.”

Richard Gowan, an expert on the U.N. at the International Crisis Group, said that Mr. Guterres wanted to leave office with a final pitch for greater international cooperation. “He has worked hard to make the U.N. address climate change, artificial intelligence and inequality more seriously,” said Mr. Gowan. “But at a time of global fragmentation, his appeals for global solidarity can fall flat.”

Two senior U.N. officials said that Mr. Guterres had spent weeks preparing his 18-page speech, which he delivered in English, French and Spanish. One of the officials said that he wanted his final address to be urgent and forward looking.

“The world does not need a weaker United Nations,” Mr. Guterres said at the end of his speech. “It needs a U.N. strong enough to face the world as it is — and determined enough to build the world as it should be.”

Mr. Guterres said he would never give up on the ideals of the U.N. and received a long applause.

item.title: Latin American Allies of Trump Plan to Label Cartels as ‘Terrorist’
item.description:
As the Trump administration tries to turn attention back to the Western Hemisphere after months of war in Iran, officials are seeking to intensify the fight against Latin American cartels.

At the United Nations General Assembly this week, State Department officials are expected to announce that 14 Latin American and Caribbean nations are labeling 25 criminal groups as terrorist organizations, according to U.S. and Latin American officials. The groups have already been labeled foreign terrorist organizations by Washington.

The move, analysts say, helps lay the groundwork for potential military strikes against criminal groups accused of drug trafficking.

The joint statement will be announced on the sidelines of the General Assembly, according to two U.S. officials, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The formal mechanism for the designation is the Rio Treaty, the officials said, a 1947 defense pact among more than a dozen nations in the Western Hemisphere that holds an attack on one member to be an attack on all.

The move would mark the first time that a group of Latin American governments has collectively signed a sweeping terrorism designation alongside Washington.

The countries signing the statement — which belong to the Shield of the Americas, an alliance of nations with conservative governments that was formed by the Trump administration — are Argentina, Bolivia, Colombia, Chile, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago.

Peru and Paraguay confirmed that they had signed the joint statement. The State Department and the governments of the other countries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Former U.S. officials and experts said the move could have sweeping effects in the region. “They’re doing it at U.N.G.A. to try to give it legitimacy,” said Todd Robinson, who was an assistant secretary of state for international narcotics and law enforcement at the State Department under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. “But I think the strategy is basically wrong. Criminal organizations are not terrorist organizations.”

Mr. Robinson said the United States had made more headway fighting traffickers in Latin America by focusing on the “civilian security apparatus that is trained to go after these organizations — to go after their money, to collect evidence, to indict and prosecute and to, under the rule of law, bring these people to justice.”

A militarized approach, by contrast, has not succeeded in curbing the flow of drugs to the United States and could result in extrajudicial killings, Mr. Robinson said. “It already has,” he said, citing lethal strikes on boats that the Trump administration, without providing evidence, said were carrying drugs.

The attacks on boats, which have killed more than 220 people, violate international law and could constitute crimes against humanity, a U.N. legal expert wrote this week.

Since President Trump returned to office, the State Department has added around 20 Latin American and Caribbean groups to the United States’ list of foreign terrorist organizations, far more than any other administration has.

The expanded list includes major cartels such as Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel; transnational gangs like Tren de Aragua, which was formed in Venezuela; and Ecuadorean gangs that U.S. officials say supply cocaine to Mexican cartels. Mr. Trump has accused the groups of attacking the United States by flooding it with drugs and with migrants whom he has linked to crime.

While the terrorist designation offers tools to freeze or seize U.S.-based assets, it does not, on its own, authorize military operations. The administration has nonetheless leaned on its designations when announcing military strikes.

The coordinated designation of the same groups as terrorist organizations by Latin American countries appears to be part of the administration’s effort to pursue such groups using military force — and to recast what critics see as a U.S.-driven agenda as a shared regional priority, said Gimena Sánchez, the Andes director for the Washington Office on Latin America, a research group.

But the designations could impinge on national sovereignty and each country’s laws governing the use of force, she added.

Labeling groups as terrorist organizations, Ms. Sánchez said, could also lead to bombings that could endanger civilians and could expand governments’ power to target citizens, enabling officials to accuse virtually anyone, including political opponents, of being “pro-terrorist” or providing support to a designated group.

Juan Pablo Segura, the assistant secretary of state for Western Hemisphere affairs, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, now special envoy to the Shield of the Americas, met last week in Washington with diplomats from 14 Latin American nations to prepare the statement.

This month, following a trip by Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, U.S. officials announced that $52 million in military aid would be shifted from certain countries in the Middle East and Europe to those three countries, as well as Panama, to combat “narcoterrorism” and secure the Panama Canal.

“These are not just criminal organizations,” Mr. Rubio said in Ecuador, describing joint operations against traffickers. “These are terrorist organizations. They have to be confronted and they have to be dismantled.”

Mitra Taj contributed reporting from Lima and Lucía Cholakian Herrera from Buenos Aires.
